entry: 16th-century Chinese novel, published during the [[Ming dynasty]] and attributed to Wu Cheng'en. It is a fictionalized, fantastic account of the 19-year pilgrimage of the Buddhist monk [[Xuanzang]] to India in the 7th century AD to collect Buddhist scriptures. The opening chapters follow [[Sun Wukong]], a monkey born from a stone egg who learns the Tao, 72 transformations and combat, and who becomes the first disciple of the monk. Three other disciples, who serve him to atone for their sins, join the journey. The novel draws on [[Taoism]], [[Buddhism]] and [[Chinese folk religion]], and combines comic adventure with satire of Chinese bureaucracy. Regarded as one of the great Chinese novels, it inspired many modern manga and anime series. Arthur Waley's 1942 abridged translation, *Monkey*, made it widely known in English-speaking countries.

English post-punk band formed in Salford in 1976. Its debut album, *Unknown Pleasures* (1979), was produced by Martin Hannett for the independent label Factory Records. Vocalist Ian Curtis, who struggled with depression and epilepsy, died by suicide in May 1980, on the eve of the band's first North American tour. The surviving members regrouped as [[New Order (band)|New Order]]. The second and final album, *Closer*, was released two months later, and its single "Love Will Tear Us Apart" became the band's highest-charting release. Joy Division remained a prominent influence on [[Alternative rock|alternative]] and gothic rock.

King of Spain, 1975–2014. Chosen as successor by [[Francisco Franco]], Juan Carlos helped dismantle the Francoist system and oversaw Spain's transition to democracy after he became king. The 1977 general election, the first free election since 1936, was followed by the Spanish Constitution of 1978, which re-established a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]]. In 1981 he played a major role in preventing a coup attempt to restore Francoist government in the King's name. His reputation suffered after controversies involving his family and an elephant-hunting trip taken during Spain's financial crisis. He abdicated in June 2014 in favor of his son, Felipe VI. Since August 2020 he has lived in self-imposed exile over allegedly improper ties to business deals in [[Saudi Arabia]].

Argentine racing driver and five-time Formula One world champion. Fangio competed in [[Formula One]] from 1950 to 1958 and, at the time of his retirement, held the records for most wins (24), pole positions (29), fastest laps (23) and podium finishes (35). He won titles with four teams: Alfa Romeo (1951), Maserati (1954 and 1957), [[Mercedes-Benz]] (1954 and 1955) and [[Ferrari]] (1956). He won 24 of the 52 Grands Prix he entered, the highest win percentage in Formula One at 46.15%, and his pole percentage of 55.77% is also the highest. In the 1955 Argentine Grand Prix, run in very hot weather, he drove the whole race alone at age 44 and set the fastest lap. He won the 1953 Carrera Panamericana and the 12 Hours of Sebring in 1956 and 1957.

Argentine military officer and politician, president of Argentina (1946–1955, 1973–1974). His movement, known as Peronism, remains a force in Argentine politics. His first administration initiated industrialization, expanded social rights, made university tuition free and granted women the right to vote. With his wife, [[Eva Perón]], he built half a million houses and gave charity, especially to children. Dissidents were fired, arrested or exiled, and the press was controlled. After attempts to sanction a divorce law and the deportation of two priests, he was mistakenly thought to have been excommunicated by the [[Catholic Church]]. In June 1955 pro-Church elements of the armed forces bombed Plaza de Mayo in [[Buenos Aires]], killing 300 civilians, and a coup later deposed him. He lived in exile in [[Paraguay]], [[Venezuela]], [[Panama]] and [[Spain]] before returning in 1973. Supporters credit the Peróns with efforts to eliminate poverty and dignify labor, while detractors call them demagogues and dictators.

Spanish explorer and conquistador. He led the first European expeditions to [[Puerto Rico]] in 1508 and to [[Florida]] in 1513. After serving as a military official on [[Hispaniola]], where he helped crush a rebellion of the [[Taíno]] people, he became the first governor of Puerto Rico in 1509. After a long court battle, Diego Colón, son of [[Christopher Columbus]], replaced him as governor in 1511. In 1513 he landed on Florida's east coast, named it La Florida and charted its Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Later stories say he sought the Fountain of Youth, but there is no contemporary evidence for this, and most historians consider it a myth. In 1521 he led the first large-scale Spanish attempt at a colony in what is now the continental United States. Calusa resistance wounded him, and he died soon after returning to [[Cuba]], the colony abandoned.

Mexican Hieronymite nun and Baroque writer, philosopher, composer and poet. Born near [[Mexico City]] as the illegitimate daughter of a Spanish navy captain, she was educated largely in her maternal grandfather's library at the Hacienda de Panoayan. Described as a child prodigy, she reportedly learned Latin at an early age and at eight composed a poem on the [[Eucharist]]. In 1664 she was sent to Mexico City and became a lady-in-waiting at the viceregal court. She was refused entry to the university, so she continued her studies privately. She has been presented as a candidate for Catholic sainthood and as a symbol of Mexican nationalism, and as a champion of [[Freedom of speech|freedom of speech]] and [[Women's rights|women's rights]].

Official state ideology of [[North Korea]]. The name derives from a Sino-Japanese word, *shutai*, meaning subject. North Korean sources credit [[Kim Il Sung]] with conceptualizing it. Juche was originally treated as a variant of [[Marxism–Leninism]], but [[Kim Jong Il]] declared it a distinct ideology in the 1970s. Official descriptions say that people are the masters of everything and decide everything. Juche emphasizes national sovereignty, self-reliance, human agency and the role of the leader. Critics describe it as a quasi-religion, a nationalist or fascistic ideology, and a deviation from Marxism–Leninism.

Czech rabbi, Talmudic scholar and Jewish mystic, known as the Maharal of Prague. He was a leading rabbi in Mikulov, Moravia, and in [[Prague]], [[Bohemia]]. He was also a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher. In 1553 he accepted a rabbinical position as Landesrabbiner of Moravia at Mikulov, where he revised community statutes on elections and taxation. He wrote on Jewish philosophy and mysticism. His supercommentary on [[Rashi]]'s commentary on the [[Torah]], *Gur Aryeh*, is among his best-known works. A later legend says he created the [[Golem]] of Prague, an animate figure of clay, but the story has no contemporary historical attestation and arose long after his death.

Disciple of [[Jesus]] who betrayed him to the authorities. According to the four canonical gospels, Judas was one of the Twelve Apostles. He identified Jesus to the Sanhedrin with a kiss in the Garden of Gethsemane, in exchange for thirty pieces of silver. The Gospel of Matthew says that he later returned the money and hanged himself. The priests used the money to buy a field called the Field of Blood. Acts, quoting Peter, says that Judas bought the field himself and died in a fall. The Gnostic Gospel of Judas, which [[Irenaeus]] denounced as heresy, portrays his actions as obedience to Jesus. Scholars widely regard Judas as a historical figure, though his motives remain a matter of interpretation. His name has become a byword for betrayal.

English heavy metal band formed in [[Birmingham]] in 1969. The band was a pioneer of the new wave of British heavy metal and an influence on speed, thrash and power metal. It struggled commercially until *British Steel* (1980) brought mainstream attention. [[The Guardian]] called *British Steel* the record that defines heavy metal. Rob Halford, who joined as vocalist in 1973, left in 1992 and returned in 2003. The band has sold over 50 million albums and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2022.

Apostle of [[Jesus]], generally identified with Thaddeus and also called Judas Thaddaeus. He is distinguished from [[Judas Iscariot]], the betrayer of Jesus. He is sometimes identified with Jude, the brother of Jesus, and with the author of the Epistle of Jude. The Armenian Apostolic Church honors him, with Saint Bartholomew, as a patron saint, and in the Catholic Church he is the patron of desperate cases and lost causes. He is commonly depicted with a [[Club (weapon)|club]], and in icons often has a flame around his head for Pentecost. Another common attribute is an image of Jesus known as the Image of Edessa.

Public official who presides over court proceedings, alone or on a judicial panel. In an adversarial system, such as those of the U.S. and England, the judge acts as an impartial referee, ensuring correct procedure, while the prosecution and defense present their cases to a [[Jury]], which finds the facts. The judge then sentences. In inquisitorial systems of continental Europe, the judge is the main fact-finder and may also act as an examining magistrate. Professional judges are legally trained; in the U.S. this generally requires a Juris Doctor, and they are often appointed from experienced attorneys. Volunteer judges, such as English magistrates, are unpaid and need no legal training. Judges are appointed or, in some jurisdictions, elected, and their rulings are subject to review by higher courts.

English actress. Dench made her professional debut in 1957 with the Old Vic Company and played Shakespearean roles, including Ophelia in *Hamlet*. Her leading role as Sally Bowles in *Cabaret* (1968) drew excellent reviews. She worked with the National Theatre Company and the Royal Shakespeare Company. She rose to international fame as M in *GoldenEye* (1995) and played the role in eight James Bond films, ending with a cameo in *Spectre* (2015). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing [[Elizabeth I|Queen Elizabeth I]] in *Shakespeare in Love* (1998).

System of courts that adjudicates legal disputes and interprets and applies the law. Under the doctrine of the [[Separation of powers|separation of powers]], the judiciary generally does not make statutory law or enforce it, although in some countries it does make common law. In many jurisdictions courts have judicial review, the power to annul laws found incompatible with the [[Constitution]], treaties or international law. Political bias and sentencing disparities reduce the judiciary's legitimacy, and public confidence varies by country, according to opinion polls. In 451–449 BC, Roman customary rules were written down in the Twelve Tables. Justinian later codified Roman law in the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*.

Modern Japanese martial art and combat sport, an Olympic sport since 1964. [[Kanō Jigorō]] created judo in 1882 as an eclectic martial art derived from [[Jujutsu|jujutsu]] schools. It emphasizes *randori* (free sparring) over *kata* (prearranged forms) and removes striking and weapon training. Its philosophy rests on *seiryoku zenyō* (maximum efficient use of energy) and *jita kyōei* (mutual welfare and benefit). In competition, a player aims to throw an opponent onto their back, pin them, or force a submission with a joint lock or choke. Judo influenced [[Brazilian jiu-jitsu]], [[Krav Maga]] and [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial arts]].

American actress, singer and vaudevillian. Born Frances Ethel Gumm, she began performing at age two with her sisters in a [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] act, the Gumm Sisters. She signed with [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] at 13 and became internationally known for playing Dorothy Gale in *The Wizard of Oz* (1939), which featured her signature song, "Over the Rainbow." Her MGM musicals included *Meet Me in St. Louis* (1944), *Easter Parade* (1948) and *Summer Stock* (1950). She received Academy Award nominations for *A Star Is Born* (1954) and *Judgment at Nuremberg* (1961). Her live album *Judy at Carnegie Hall* (1961) made her the first woman to win the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for Album of the Year. Dependencies on prescription medications affected her health, and she died from an accidental [[Barbiturate|barbiturate]] overdose.

American lawyer and court-show arbitrator. After serving as a New York family-court prosecutor, she was appointed a criminal-court judge by Mayor Ed Koch in 1982 and became a supervising judge in 1986. Her fame grew after a 1993 *Los Angeles Times* profile and a segment on CBS's *60 Minutes*. She starred in *Judge Judy* for 25 seasons, from 1996 to 2021, the longest-serving television arbitrator in courtroom programming, a record recognized by [[Guinness World Records]]. She won six Daytime Emmy Awards and a Lifetime Achievement Emmy in 2019. In September 2026 she announced her retirement, with the finale of *Judy Justice* on October 22.

Drink made from the liquid extracted or pressed from fruits or vegetables. The term can also refer to liquids flavored with concentrate or with meat or seafood, such as clam juice. Juice became popular after [[Pasteurization|pasteurization]] allowed it to be stored without [[Fermentation|fermenting]] into alcohol. Grape pits dated to 8000 BCE show early evidence of juice production, and lemonade appeared in 16th-century Italy. In 1869 the dentist Thomas B. Welch developed a pasteurization method and sold the product as "Dr. Welch's Unfermented Wine." After James Lind linked citrus fruit to the prevention of [[Scurvy|scurvy]] in the 18th century, the Merchant Shipping Act 1867 required British ocean-going ships to carry citrus-based juice. In the United States, a product may be called fruit juice only if it is 100% juice; blends with sweeteners are called juice cocktails or juice drinks.

Private conservatory for the performing arts in New York City. Founded in 1905 by Frank Damrosch as the Institute of Musical Art, it was renamed for its principal benefactor, Augustus D. Juilliard, and later added dance and drama divisions. The music division is the largest and oldest. The school occupies a single campus at Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts and has one of the lowest acceptance rates of U.S. schools. Its alumni have won 105 [[Grammy Awards]], 62 Tony Awards, 47 Emmy Awards and 24 [[Academy Awards]]. Its alumni and faculty include more than 16 Pulitzer Prize and 12 National Medal of Arts recipients.

Tree or shrub, *Ziziphus jujuba*, of the buckthorn family, cultivated for its edible fruit. Thought to have originated in eastern Asia, it tolerates climates from temperate to tropical. The fruit, also called red date or Chinese date, is eaten fresh or dried and candied. Immature fruit is smooth and green, maturing brown to purplish-black and wrinkling like a small date. The species was first named by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753 as *Rhamnus zizyphus*. It is often confused with the closely related Indian jujube, *Z. mauritiana*.

Japanese martial art and close-combat system, also spelled jiu-jitsu or ju-jitsu. The word means roughly "yielding art," reflecting a philosophy of turning an opponent's force against them. Jujutsu developed as a way to defeat armored [[Samurai|samurai]] without weapons. Because striking armor proved ineffective, its methods relied on pins, joint locks and throws. Its schools teach grappling, strikes and often weapons. A subset of its techniques influenced [[Judo]], aikido, hapkido, sambo, [[Brazilian jiu-jitsu]] and [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial arts]]. Judo was developed by [[Kanō Jigorō]] in the late 19th century from several traditional jujutsu styles.

French novelist, poet and playwright, sometimes called the father of [[Science fiction]]. Born in [[Nantes]], he collaborated with the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel on the *Voyages extraordinaires*, a series of adventure novels including *Journey to the Center of the Earth* (1864), *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas* (1870) and *Around the World in Eighty Days* (1872). His novels are generally set in the second half of the 19th century and draw on contemporary science. Verne is an important author in [[France]] and most of Europe, but in the Anglosphere he was often labeled a writer of children's books, largely because of abridged translations. He has been the second most-translated author in the world since 1979, after [[Agatha Christie]] and ahead of [[William Shakespeare]].

American chef, author and television personality. She brought [[French cuisine]] to American audiences with her debut cookbook, *Mastering the Art of French Cooking*, and with *The French Chef*, which premiered in 1963 and ran for almost ten years. At 6 feet 2 inches, she was too tall to enlist in the Women's Army Corps or the Navy's WAVES, and in 1942 she joined the Office of Strategic Services. She worked on a shark repellent intended to keep sharks from setting off underwater explosives aimed at German [[U-boat|U-boats]]. She learned to cook after meeting her husband, Paul, who grew up in a family interested in food.

American actress and comedian. She was a cast member of *Saturday Night Live* from 1982 to 1985 and gained wide recognition as Elaine Benes on the [[NBC]] [[Sitcom|sitcom]] *Seinfeld* (1990–1998). She later starred as Selina Meyer in *Veep* (2012–2019). She has won eleven Primetime Emmy Awards, nine Actor Awards and a Golden Globe Award, and she has won more Actor Awards than any other performer. She has played Valentina Allegra de Fontaine in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] since 2021.
